pages.text: Rock buried deep recrystallises into whatever is stable down there. The $(item)Tectonic Press$() does it on purpose: a multi-anvil vessel over a firebox, under a hydraulic ram. You set two things - the anvil pressure and the furnace temperature - and the phase diagram does the rest.

Each boundary between two minerals is a line on that diagram, and its slope is the $(thing)Clapeyron slope$(), dP/dT = ΔS/ΔV. Graphite turns to diamond above P = 1.94 + 0.0025·T(°C) GPa; olivine to ringwoodite above about 17.5 GPa; ringwoodite to bridgmanite above the post-spinel line near 23 GPa, which leans the other way.

Being on the right side is not enough: the sample must be hot enough to react. Its rate follows Arrhenius - a few hundred kelvin make the difference between hours and seconds. Diamond also wants a solvent: keep a block of $(item)Iron-Nickel$() in the press, as real diamond presses use molten iron and nickel.
At low pressure and 3,000 K the press turns coal into nuclear-grade $(item)Graphite$(), and with brine and iron into $(item)Boron Control Rods$(): boron carbide is made the same way.
